turns.text: All right. Could you give me a brief overview of yourself and what you've been working on recently?

Sure. So, the short version is: I'm a backend engineer with about five and a half years of experience. Most of my work has been in Java and Kotlin, with PostgreSQL and Kafka. For the last three years, I've been at RouteSpan—a freight-tech product company in India. I work on shipment pricing and event ingestion. We're a nine-engineer team, and our services see events for around sixty thousand shipments on a typical day. The main thing I worked on this year was pulling carrier-rate calculation out of a large order service. I owned the service boundary, the migration plan, and most of the backend work. We moved callers gradually, checked the old and new results side by side, and then cut over. Before RouteSpan, I spent two and a half years on retail order APIs at an IT services company. What I'm looking for now is deeper product ownership—and, honestly, a team that works well in writing.

turns.text: Thanks. You said you owned the migration. What did you personally decide, versus what the team decided together?

The decision to extract pricing was already made, so I can't claim that part. What I owned was the new API and the compatibility plan. Two other engineers shared the database and deployment work with me. The final cutover criteria were a team decision with our product manager and staff engineer.

turns.text: The role is hands-on. It isn't an architecture-only role, so that part aligns. I do want to check one thing: our teams tend to give engineers fairly ambiguous problem statements. How comfortable are you with that?

More comfortable than I was two years ago. Back then, I treated ambiguity as a reason to build something very flexible—which usually meant too much. On the pricing migration, for example, I proposed three pricing strategies. Product had evidence for one. My staff engineer challenged me on that, and we cut almost a week of unnecessary work. Now I write down the unknowns first. Then I ask: which of these could actually change the design? I still want a clear outcome, but I don't need somebody to hand me every step.

turns.text: What did you change because the overlap was limited?

The first thing I changed was my end-of-day update. I included the request, what I was seeing, and the decision I needed from them. At first, those updates were way too long—almost like incident reports. People read the detail and missed the actual question. So I cut the format down to four things: the decision, my recommendation, one supporting link, and the deadline. We also moved interface questions into one shared document instead of spreading them across email and chat. Most mornings, I could start with an answer instead of waiting another day.

turns.text: Can you give me an example where async communication didn't work?

Yes. I once wrote that a field was "optional," but I didn't define what optional meant. Could it be absent? Could it be null? Could it be an empty string? I left that unclear. The partner sent null, and our side rejected it. That cost us about a day—and that one was on me. I updated the contract with explicit examples and added consumer tests for all three cases. Since then, I don't rely on words like "optional." I show valid and invalid payloads.
